title: Traders in pain
takeaway: Give your heart fully, and let the river decide whether you sink or cross.
scene: The poet describes what lovers are like: sighing, burning, carrying their pain from place to place like travelling traders. Then the beloved suddenly walks into his courtyard.

original: سینے دے وچ ٹھنڈیاں ہاواں اکھیاں وچ انگارے
دوہرے بھار نے چکی پھردے درداں دے ونجارے
transliteration: Seene de vich thandiyaan haavaan, akhiyaan vich angaare
Dohre bhaar ne chukki phirde dardaan de vanjaare
translation: Cold sighs in the chest, burning coals in the eyes:
these traders in pain wander about carrying a double load.
couplets.story: Lovers have cold, heavy sighs in their chests and eyes that burn like hot coals. They're like travelling sellers who carry their pain from town to town, and their load is twice as heavy as anyone else's.

original: دل دی بیڑی نال خشی دے شوہ حوالے کیتی
ہن اگوں دریا دی مرضی ڈوب چھڈے یا تارے
transliteration: Dil di beri naal khushi de shauh havaale keeti
Hun aggon dariya di marzi, dob chhade ya taare
translation: I gladly handed the boat of my heart over to the deep water.
Now it's up to the river whether it drowns me or carries me across.
couplets.story: He pushed the little boat of his heart into the deep river, and he did it happily. What happens next isn't up to him. The river can sink him or take him safely to the other side.

original: ہجراں مارے پوہ مہینے رہندے سڑدے بلدے
ہاڑ مہینے سینے ٹھارے تیرے اک اشارے
transliteration: Hijraan maare Poh maheene rehnde sarde balde
Haarh maheene seene thaare tere ik ishaare
translation: Those struck by separation keep burning even in freezing Poh,
while one signal from you can cool the chest in the heat of Haarh.
couplets.story: Missing the beloved makes lovers burn, even in the coldest month of winter. But one small sign from the beloved can cool them down, even in the hottest month of summer.

original: عاشق دھوناں چکی پھردے مقتل وچ بے خوفے
پئے اڈیکن اوس گھڑی نوں کد اوہ تیغ الارے
transliteration: Aashiq dhauṇaan chukki phirde maqtal vich be-khaufe
Pae udeekan os ghari nu kad oh tegh ulaare
translation: Lovers walk fearless through the place of execution, heads held high,
waiting for the moment the beloved raises the sword.
couplets.story: Lovers walk into the place of execution with their heads up, not scared at all. They're waiting for the beloved to raise the sword, as if being struck by the one they love would be an honour.

original: صوفی عابد ویکھ نہ سکے پردار ہیا جمالوں
عاشق لوکی سولی چڑھ کے کردے رہن نظارے
transliteration: Sufi aabid vekh na sake, parda reha jamaalon
Aashiq loki sooli charh ke karde rehan nazaare
translation: The Sufi and the worshipper couldn't see; beauty stayed veiled from them.
But the lovers, climbing the gallows, kept on gazing.
couplets.story: Even very religious people, who pray and worship a lot, couldn't see the beloved's beauty. It stayed hidden from them. The lovers saw it, but only by being willing to climb the gallows. Like Mansur, they paid with their lives to see.

original: سن کے درد کہانی میری جھلا کہہ کے ٹریا
پہلاں چسکے لے کے سوہنا بھردا رہیا ہنگارے
transliteration: Sun ke dard kahaani meri jhalla keh ke turiya
Pehlaan chaske lai ke sohna bharda rehiya hungaare
translation: After hearing my sad story, he called me crazy and walked off,
though at first my lovely one enjoyed it, nodding along.
couplets.story: He told the beloved his whole sad story. At first the beloved seemed interested, saying 'mm-hmm' and enjoying it. Then they called him crazy and walked away.

original: اچن اچیتی ماہی میرا آ ویہڑے وچ وڑیا
جی آیاں نوں کہندیاں کھڑ پئے پھٹ جگر دے سارے
transliteration: Achan acheti maahi mera aa vehre vich variya
Ji aayaan nu kehndiyaan khir pae phatt jigar de saare
translation: Out of nowhere my beloved walked into my courtyard,
and as I said 'welcome', every wound in my heart burst into bloom.
couplets.story: Then, without warning, the beloved walked into his courtyard. As he said 'welcome', all the wounds in his heart opened up like flowers blooming. The pain and the joy came together.

original: رنگ روپ توں ویکھ نہ ڈھلیں جھوٹیاں دولتاں اتے
ہر شے سونا تے نئیں ہوندی جیہڑی چمکاں مارے
transliteration: Rang roop ton vekh na dhaleen jhoothiyaan daulataan utte
Har shai sona te nahin hondi jehri chamkaan maare
translation: Don't melt at the sight of looks, or for false riches:
not everything that glitters is gold.
couplets.story: He warns the reader. Don't fall for good looks or fake wealth. Not everything shiny is gold.

original: ہرجائی کہہ دینا سوکھا کون دلاں دیاں جانے
رساں وی سولی تے چڑھ کے جیہڑے کرن گزارے
transliteration: Harjaai keh dena saukha, kaun dilaan diyaan jaane
Rasaan vi sooli te charh ke jehre karan guzaare
translation: It's easy to call someone unfaithful, but who knows what's in their heart?
Some get by even while climbing the gallows rope.
couplets.story: It's easy to call someone a cheat. But who really knows what's going on inside a person? Some people are quietly holding on while going through the worst things imaginable.

original: پتھر دل انساناں اتے ہر کوئی پھل برساوے
پھلاں نالوں نازک دلاں تے ہر کوئی پتھر مارے
transliteration: Patthar dil insaanaan utte har koi phull barsaave
Phullaan naalon naazak dilaan te har koi patthar maare
translation: Everyone showers flowers on people with hearts of stone,
and everyone throws stones at hearts gentler than flowers.
couplets.story: He points out something unfair about the world. People praise and reward the hard-hearted. And the gentle, sensitive people, softer than flowers, are the ones who get stones thrown at them.

original: رب کرے تے میں وی احمدؔ نال اوہناں رل جاواں
اشک جنہاں دے موتی بن دے یا بن جاون تارے
transliteration: Rab kare te main vi Ahmad naal ohnaan ral jaavaan
Ashk jinhaan de moti bande ya ban jaavan taare
translation: God willing, Ahmad, I too will join those
whose tears become pearls or turn into stars.
couplets.story: He ends with a prayer. He hopes he'll be counted among the people whose tears turn into something precious, pearls or stars, so that their pain becomes something beautiful.

deeper:
This is a map of the Sufi path. Handing the 'boat of the heart' to the river is tawakkul, complete trust in God: you do your part and leave the outcome to Him. The couplet about the Sufi and the worshipper makes a pointed claim. Religious routine alone may leave God's beauty (jamal) veiled, while the lover who gives up his ego, symbolised by the gallows, sees it.

The Beloved stepping into the courtyard 'out of nowhere' is how Sufis describe grace: closeness to God comes as a gift, not as wages for effort. The final prayer, that tears become pearls or stars, is the hope that sorrow felt for God's sake is turned into light.
why: It mixes big spiritual ideas with everyday wisdom, such as 'not everything that glitters is gold' and 'people throw stones at gentle hearts'.
prompt: Is there something in your life you've done your best on and now have to leave to God, or to time?
notes: Couplet 9, line 2 ('rasaan vi sooli te charh ke…') is the least certain line in this poem.
